newsitem.title: FRANCE: French audit incorporates Socialist measures.
newsitem.headline: French audit incorporates Socialist measures.

text.p: An audit of public finances released on Monday incorporates the cost of the Socialist-led government's first spending measures initially announced on July 9, the auditors said in their report.

The auditors said their assessment also took account of the fact the 11.1 billion francs in new spending was financed by cancelling spending plans frozen by the previous conservative government. Because of this, the auditors said the new spending measures were budget neutral.
The audit, carried out by two members of the Court of Auditors, was littered with disclaimers and warnings about the partial availability of figures for their study.
They said it was hard to establish the exact state of the accounts because many government bodies and authorities do not publish mid-year account assessments.
They said non-tax receipts were "erratic" and tough to forecast and added that, although tax receipts were usually more easily assessed, the economic situation on which they rely was not.
The auditors also noted that spending in France was so diverse as to "make a failure" of statistical analysis.
"Therefore, we had to abandon the simple method of assessment and enter the labyrinth of budgetary forecasting," the auditors wrote.
With regard to the welfare accounts, the auditors wrote.
"It quickly became apparent that it would not be possible to establish a mid-year assessment: the available intra-year statistics are clearly insufficient to make a reliable judgement."
The auditors said another problem in trying to establish the state of the welfare accounts is that they had to rely on economic forecasts made by national statistics institute INSEE in June.
"Like all forecasts, these have risks," the auditors wrote.

When forecasting the surplus in local authority budgets, the auditors said again the information was spotty. They added that it would be dangerous to count on future local authority surpluses because of changes to the economic situation.
